title: Mute one player, hear what breaks
allegory: Ablation is muting one player in an orchestra and listening to how much worse the piece gets; pure silence throws everyone off, so a fairer test has a stand-in play that player's usual part.
map: the model doing a task, scored by its loss

chapters.name: Who carries this?
chapters.note: pretty attention patterns ... but are they doing it?

cap.1: A model can repeat a pattern it saw earlier in the text. It has dozens of little parts. Which ones are actually doing the trick?
cap.2: Your two-layer model predicts the second copy of a repeated random sequence almost perfectly. Attention patterns suggest suspects; you still need a causal test.
cap.3: Attention patterns and direct logit attribution are correlational, and DLA misses indirect paths entirely: the previous-token head's contribution never reaches the logits directly.

cap.1: To find out who matters, mute one player at a time and listen. If the piece falls apart, that player was carrying something important.
cap.2: Ablation: remove one component's output with a hook, rerun, and measure how much the loss goes up. Do it for every head and you get a map of importance.
cap.3: ARENA hooks z, the per-head output before W_O, zeroes one head at a time across all layers and heads, and records each loss increase in an (n_layers, n_heads) score.

cap.1: The score is simple: how much worse it sounds with the player muted, compared with everyone playing. A big gap means an important player.
cap.2: Compute loss_no_ablation first from a clean run, then one ablated run per head. The difference, head by head, fills the score tensor.
cap.3: Ablation measures necessity for this metric under this intervention. The baseline must be genuinely unablated: call model.reset_hooks() before computing it.

chapters.name: Silence or stand-in

left.title: zero-ablation
lines: a sound the band never heard

right.title: mean-ablation
lines: a stand-in plays the usual part

chapters.verdict: Replace with the mean over a reference set, not with zero.

cap.1: Pure silence is strange for a band that has always heard that part, so everyone stumbles. A stand-in playing the usual part is a fairer test.
cap.2: Zeroing an activation puts the model somewhere it has never been, which overstates the damage. Mean-ablation over a reference distribution keeps it on-distribution.
cap.3: Zero is rarely a typical value for an activation; mean-ablation removes only the input-specific information. [1.2] has you implement both and compare them.

cap.1: Ablation can fool you both ways. Mute the player who hands out the sheet music and everything breaks. Mute a star and an understudy quietly covers.
cap.2: Knocking out MLP0 in GPT-2 small wrecks almost any task because it acts like an extended embedding. In IOI, backup name movers take over when the main ones are ablated.
cap.3: Big damage need not mean task-specific (MLP0); small damage need not mean unimportant (backup heads). Under redundancy, single-head ablation systematically understates importance.

chapters.name: Which test, when
items: Now: mean-ablation over a reference set
Sharper: patch in a specific alternative

cap.1: Muting is the bluntest test. Swapping in what a player did on a different song asks a sharper question. For a huge band, estimate every seat at once.
cap.2: Current method: mean-ablation. Activation patching replaces with a specific alternative, a sharper causal question. Attribution patching approximates it with gradients, far cheaper.
cap.3: Ablation turns 'this head looks important' into a causal claim. Use mean-ablation for [1.2], patching when you have a clean/corrupted pair, attribution patching to triage, then verify the top hits.

where_else: Finding a minimal circuit: ablate everything outside it and check performance survives
Activation patching: the same surgery with a specific replacement instead of a blank
Ablation studies in ML papers: drop one design choice and compare
Gene knockouts in biology, with the same trap of redundant backups

hamming.what: Removing one component's output, by zeroing it or replacing it with its mean, and measuring how much performance drops.
hamming.when: When you have a suspect component and want a first causal test of whether the model needs it.
hamming.why: Attention patterns only show correlation; knocking a part out shows necessity, as long as you watch for off-distribution shock and for backups covering.

object.title: The damage map
object.subtitle: One bar per player: how much worse the piece gets when that player alone is muted.

cap.1: Each bar is how much worse the music gets when that one player is muted. A few tall bars, many short ones.
cap.2: A (layers, heads) score map: the loss increase when each head alone is mean-ablated. Toy values.
cap.3: score[l, h] = L(ablate l.h) - L(clean), replacing with the mean over a reference distribution.

cap.1: Mute with pure silence instead of a stand-in and every bar grows: the band is thrown by a sound it has never heard.
cap.2: Zero-ablation inflates scores: zero is off-distribution, so part of the damage is shock, not the head.
cap.3: The uniform offset is a toy; real zero-ablation bias varies with how far 0 sits from each component's typical values.

cap.1: The tallest bar is the player who hands out the sheet music. Mute them and everything breaks, whatever the piece.
cap.2: Like MLP0 in GPT-2 small, which acts as an extended embedding: huge damage on any task, so not task-specific.
cap.3: Necessity across every task signals infrastructure, not circuit membership. Compare against other tasks before concluding.

cap.1: Now mute the understudy as well, and the star's bar shoots up. Alone, the star looked minor only because someone covered.
cap.2: Backup heads mask importance: in IOI, backup name movers take over when the primary movers are ablated.
cap.3: Redundancy makes single-component ablation understate importance; ablate sets of components to expose it.

cap.1: Tall bars point to suspects, not verdicts. Next, swap in specific alternatives to ask sharper questions.
cap.2: Ablation is a first pass. Activation patching and path patching ask narrower causal questions.
cap.3: Treat the score map as triage; confirm with patching, and check for both over- and under-statement before naming a circuit.

predict.q: Zero-ablating a head gives a big loss jump; mean-ablating it gives a small one. Which is the fairer estimate?
predict.why: Zero is a value the model has never seen there, so part of the damage is shock. Mean-ablation removes only the input-specific part.

predict.q: Muting the star barely hurts. Muting star and understudy together wrecks the piece. What does that say about the star?

options.t: It matters; its backup was hiding that

predict.why: Backups cover for ablated components, so single ablations understate importance, as with backup name movers in IOI.

predict.q: Your head-ablation sweep returns almost all zeros with a few small negatives. Most likely?

options.t: A stale hook is still attached, so the baseline was already ablated
No head in the model matters

predict.why: Hooks are global model state. Call model.reset_hooks() before computing the clean baseline.

object.where: Any system with redundant parts: knocking one out tests necessity, never sufficiency, and backups can hide it.
